quote: The phlogiston theory of chemistry could explain just about anything, so long as it didn’t have to predict it in advance.
content: This is the sixth appearance of the claim in the book, and it was false the first time. Phlogiston theory predicted that metals would lose weight on calcination, that combustion would cease in a sealed vessel when the air was saturated, that the calx could be restored to metal by heating with a phlogiston-rich substance such as charcoal, and that "inflammable air" (hydrogen) would reduce calxes; the first prediction failed and the others succeeded, which is what a theory that makes predictions looks like. The Book I annotations set out the history. The essay's opening example of an unfalsifiable theory is a falsified one, which is a different thing, and the difference is the subject of the chapter in Book I where the confusion was first introduced.

quote: Positive characteristics enhance perception of every other positive characteristic? That sounds a lot like how a fissioning uranium atom sends out neutrons that fission other uranium atoms.
content: No study has measured the iterative amplification the metaphor describes. The halo effect as documented is a one-shot cross-trait influence: a manipulated warmth or attractiveness cue shifts ratings of other traits in a single judgment (Nisbett & Wilson 1977), and nothing in that literature shows the shifted trait feeding back to raise the original cue. The escalation the essay wants to explain, people becoming more extreme over time about a cause, has a well-studied mechanism that is social rather than intrapersonal: group polarization, in which discussion among the like-minded moves the group's average toward the extreme through persuasive-arguments and social-comparison processes (Myers & Lamm 1976). The essay reaches for a chain reaction inside one head when the field had located the reaction between heads. The next essay's own examples, the Objectivists and the mailing list, are group phenomena.
